description: KinetiCore is a one-person team driven by curiosity about space, science, and technology. As the founder and sole member, I combine software development, data visualization, research, and creative problem-solving to turn complex ideas into accessible prototypes. I learn quickly, test assumptions, and build practical tools with users in mind. For NASA Space Apps, OrbitForge aims to connect open space data with meaningful decisions on Earth and beyond.
summary:
Kinetic Core is a browser-based 3D spaceflight game that I developed independently to turn space exploration into interactive learning. I created a rocket-design workshop and flight exercises covering launch, stage separation, orbital docking, and planetary landings. A separate Earth free-flight mode lets players pilot a rocket above real geographic maps, change direction and altitude, manage fuel, land, and take off again.

The project makes space science more accessible through experimentation. Players discover how gravity, thrust, momentum, and fuel consumption affect flight. NASA/JPL reference data inform the landing environments, while open geographic data provide recognizable Earth locations. Clear instruments, a rotating 3D camera, and intuitive controls help players connect their actions with visible consequences.

Kinetic Core encourages curiosity, problem-solving, and persistence. Failed landings become opportunities to understand excessive speed, uncontrolled drift, or limited fuel and improve the next attempt. Its browser-based format simplifies access and supports demonstrations and independent exploration. My goal is to make the engineering decisions behind space missions understandable and engaging, inspiring players to explore science and technology through hands-on play.
details:
Kinetic Core is a browser-based 3D spaceflight game that I developed as an independent creator. Its purpose is to make space science and engineering easier to understand through experimentation and interactive flight exercises.

The project combines a rocket-design workshop with activities covering launch, stage separation, orbital docking, and planetary landings. A separate Earth free-flight mode lets players pilot a 3D rocket above real geographic maps, control its direction and altitude, manage fuel, land, and take off again. Flight instruments display information such as altitude, speed, and remaining propellant, while a 360-degree camera allows players to inspect their spacecraft and surroundings.

The game encourages learning through consequences. Excessive speed, uncontrolled drift, or insufficient fuel can cause a failed landing, giving players a reason to reconsider their approach. Its intended impact is to encourage curiosity about space exploration, develop problem-solving skills, and make scientific concepts more approachable.

I used JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with Three.js for 3D graphics and Vite for development and production builds. MapLibre GL JS, OpenFreeMap, OpenStreetMap, and Mapzen terrain data support the Earth environment. NASA/JPL planetary reference data inform the planetary landing exercises. GitHub stores the source code, and GitHub Pages provides public access to the game.

The project’s creative approach combines spacecraft construction, interactive physics, and recognizable geographic locations in one browser-based experience. During development, I considered accessibility without installation, clear controls, laptop performance, meaningful feedback, and the limitations of geographic data. The spacecraft hardware and some physics are simplified for gameplay. Construction, orbital exercises, and Earth free flight currently remain separate activities rather than one continuous mission.
